Holy Convocation
HO-lee kon-vuh-KAY-shun
noun phrase / Hebrew term
Holy (Old English halig, set apart, consecrated, whole; cognate with German heilig; the concept of sacred separation and dedication to God) + convocation (from Latin convocatio, a calling together, from convocare: con-, together + vocare, to call). The phrase translates Hebrew miqra’ qōdesh (miqra’, something called out or a sacred assembly, from qara’, to call; qōdesh, holiness or the set-apart state). The term appears first in Leviticus 23:2–4 as the defining character of Israel's appointed feasts: they are not self-organized gatherings but divinely called assemblies.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The holy convocation (miqra’ qōdesh) is the assembly that God calls out from the ordinary course of life for the purpose of covenant worship — a gathering whose authority, timing, and character derive from God's call rather than human initiative. Leviticus 23:2 introduces the entire appointed-times calendar with this designation: the mo’adim are “holy convocations” — times at which Israel is not merely invited but called, as a community, into the LORD's presence for a set purpose. The weekly Sabbath is explicitly named a “holy convocation” (Lev 23:3), establishing the pattern from the most regular assembly to the most solemn annual one. Each major feast — the first and last days of Unleavened Bread (Lev 23:7–8), Pentecost (Num 28:26), Trumpets (Lev 23:24), Atonement (Lev 23:27), and the first and eighth days of Tabernacles (Lev 23:35, 36) — is a holy convocation. The holy convocation required “no customary work” (Num 28:18) — the ordinary labor of the week is suspended because God has called the community out of that ordinary into something extraordinary. Isaiah 1:13 records the LORD's rebuke of corrupt convocations: “Bring no more futile sacrifices; incense is an abomination to Me. The New Moons, the Sabbaths, and the calling of assemblies — I cannot endure iniquity and the sacred meeting.” This verse establishes a critical principle: the holy convocation is desecrated when the assembly brings iniquity with it. The form without the reality of covenant fidelity becomes an abomination. The New Testament fulfillment of the holy convocation is the church's weekly gathering in Christ's name (Matt 18:20; Heb 10:25) — a community called out of the world by the risen Christ, in whose presence the assembly meets.

Webster 1828 Definition

The holy convocation (miqra’ qōdesh) is the divinely called assembly of the covenant community, mandated at each appointed feast and the weekly Sabbath, in which Israel was called out of ordinary life into the presence of the LORD for worship, remembrance, and covenant renewal.

expand to see more

HOLY CONVOCATION. Hebrew miqra’ qōdesh: a divinely called sacred assembly; the designation given to the weekly Sabbath and to the opening and closing days of each major feast in the Mosaic covenant calendar (Lev 23:3, 7, 8, 21, 24, 27, 35, 36; Num 28:18, 25, 26).

2. The name is theologically programmatic: miqra’ (from qara’, to call or summon) means the assembly is constituted by God's call, not the people's convenience or decision. The New Testament church's name ekklēsia (called-out ones) is the direct Greek equivalent — the community defined by the divine summons that brought it into being.

3. The no-customary-work prohibition: each holy convocation suspended ordinary labor (Num 28:18, 25, 26; Lev 23:3, 7–8) — the economic world was set aside because God had called the community to something that relativized all ordinary priorities. Work will resume; the holy convocation will not recur until the next appointed time.

4. Isaiah 1:13 — the corrupted convocation: God rejects convocations that bring iniquity with them. The assembly that maintains all the correct forms while harboring unrepentant covenant unfaithfulness becomes an abomination rather than a holy convocation. The form of gathered worship is not automatically holy; it becomes holy when it is the genuine response of a community whose heart is toward the LORD.

5. New Testament fulfillment: the church is the eschatological holy convocation — the called-out community (Matt 16:18; Acts 2:47) that gathers in Christ's name (Matt 18:20), under His priestly presidency (Heb 8:1–2), for Word and ordinance. Hebrews 10:25 makes the weekly assembly a moral obligation: “not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together.”

Key Scripture

Lev 23:2 — "Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: The appointed feasts of the LORD which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, these are My feasts."

Lev 23:3 — "Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work on it; it is the Sabbath of the LORD in all your dwellings."

Num 28:18 — "On the first day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall do no customary work."

Isa 1:13 — "Bring no more futile sacrifices; incense is an abomination to Me. The New Moons, the Sabbaths, and the calling of assemblies — I cannot endure iniquity and the sacred meeting."

Modern Corruption

The holy convocation has been corrupted in modern evangelical practice by the consumer-church model that replaces the divinely called assembly with an audience-experience — transforming the miqra’ qōdesh from a covenant obligation of the community to an optional personal enrichment event for individual spiritual consumers.

expand to see more

The ancient corruption is Isaiah's: attending the form of the sacred assembly while bringing iniquity with it — the Sabbath observed externally while the heart pursues exploitation and injustice (Isa 58:3–7). God rejects this convocation as more offensive than no convocation at all (Isa 1:13–15). The modern church faces the same corruption in multiple guises: the congregation that maintains worship services while tolerating unrepentant sin in its membership; the church that holds theologically correct forms while its leadership harbors pride and self-aggrandizement; the worship gathering that performs the externals of reverence while the congregation's hearts are far from God (Isa 29:13). The miqra’ qōdesh demands not only the form of assembly but the reality of a community that has come clean before the LORD.

The more modern corruption is the dissolution of assembly itself into a consumer experience. The theological category of holy convocation is a called-out, gathered, covenantal community with obligations to each other and to the Lord of the assembly. The consumer-church model reconstitutes this as an audience that attends performances and exits without covenant bonds. “Forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) becomes normalized; the covenant community's weekly gathering is replaced by personal spiritual content consumed on individual schedules. The church is not an audience God addresses; it is a covenant people God assembles.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The holy convocation roots in Israel's covenant-assembly pattern throughout the wilderness (Numbers 10's trumpet-summoned assemblies) and the Mosaic feast-calendar (Lev 23), in the Psalms of Ascent as the pilgrimage-assembly spirituality, and in the New Testament church as the eschatological fulfillment of the called-out covenant community.

expand to see more

Hebrew miqra’ (from qara’, to call or summon): the assembly constituted by divine call, not human organization; its authority derives from the One who summons, not the organizational capacity of the gathered

Numbers 10:1–10 — the silver trumpet protocol: God commands Moses to make two silver trumpets for summoning the assembly and for signaling the march; the trumpet-call is God's initiative calling Israel out of their tents into the covenant gathering

Leviticus 23 — the feast-calendar as the annual schedule of holy convocations: seven assemblies plus the weekly Sabbath, each marked by cessation of ordinary labor and gathering for the LORD's appointed purpose

Psalms 84 and 122 — the assembly-longing psalms: “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!” (Ps 84:1); “I was glad when they said to me, let us go into the house of the LORD” (Ps 122:1); the affective dimension of holy convocation — not duty alone but delight

New Testament ekklēsia — Matt 16:18; 18:20; Acts 2:42–47: the church as the eschatological holy convocation; constituted by Christ's call, gathered in His name, under His priestly mediation, for Word and ordinance and mutual covenant care

Usage

"The theological weight of Leviticus 23:2 — “these are My feasts” — transfers directly to the New Testament church's Lord's Day assembly. The gathered church does not belong to the pastor, to the congregation's preference, or to the broader culture's scheduling calendar; it is the LORD's holy convocation, shaped by His agenda, under His authority, for the purpose He has appointed."

"Isaiah 1:13's rebuke of corrupted convocations provides the diagnostic question for every gathered church: does the assembly actually bring the community into the presence of a holy God for genuine covenant renewal, or does it bring the forms of worship as a covering for covenant unfaithfulness? The corrupted convocation is worse than no convocation — it is presumption made liturgical. Church discipline and congregational accountability are the institutional safeguards that maintain the difference between a holy convocation and a religious performance."

"Hebrews 10:25 — “not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” — is the New Testament's direct application of the holy-convocation principle to the church's weekly Lord's Day gathering. The verse does not say “not merely reducing the frequency of your attendance”; it says “not forsaking,” a verb used in Hebrews for the abandonment of a covenant commitment. The weekly assembly is not a spiritual enhancement option; it is the covenant community's regular constitutive act."
